<reason>Side B (PRO) won on the strength of a single, sustained, decisive reframe: every harm CON predicts is a person reacting rationally to a true fact, so CON's remedy is always that fewer people know the truth. Side A fought back well — the diner-menu "accurate numbers that mislead" analogy, the decision-irrelevance of the rider's price to dollars-per-mile math, and the outlier-screenshot path to commission caps were genuinely live counters, and A answered B's pressure questions directly and cleanly (A4.1/A4.2). But B's answers held: the tenant/landlord analogy (B4.1) neutralized the "misinformation without context" charge by noting a hidden number has no context at all; the subsidy display ("platform contribution $3") undercut the cross-subsidy freeze claim; and B's closing line "If the split survives daylight, disclosure costs nothing. If it doesn't, that was the point" crystallized the burden in a way A's closing never overturned. A's strongest route — that the split is decision-irrelevant for drivers — was blunted by B's platform-comparison and margin-squeeze point, which A answered only by assertion. B's slightly clipped opening was a minor execution cost with no substantive loss. Clear but competitive edge to B.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was B's Rebuttal 1 ([B2.1]) — "nearly every harm it predicts depends on people discovering things that are true" — which A attempted to counter with the diner-menu/context argument, only for B to close the door in Rebuttal 2 ([B4.1]-[B4.4]) with the tenant/landlord analogy and the "managed ignorance" concession frame that A's closing could only restate against, not defeat.</best_rebuttal>
